SK6023 A type has no members, no base and no attributes

A class Foo { } that derives from nothing, carries no attribute and declares nothing is a declaration that was started and not finished.

CategoryDesign
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS2094

Why

An empty type is usually one of four things, and three of them are legitimate patterns: a marker attribute, a marker interface, a named specialisation of a generic base, or the leftovers of an edit. Only the fourth is a finding, and the first three are all recognisable from the declaration itself — an attribute has a base or an attribute list, a marker interface is an interface, and a specialisation has a base list. What is left is a type with nothing attached to it in any direction: no members, no base, no interfaces, no attributes, no type parameters, not partial. That is not a marker, because nothing can key on it; it is a name and a pair of braces. Either it is about to become something and the declaration landed early, or it stopped being something and the members were deleted around it.

Example

Instead of:

public sealed class OrderProcessor { }

Write:

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public sealed class AuditedAttribute : Attribute { }

When it does not fire

The exemptions are the rule. A detector for "no members" is three lines; deciding which empty types are deliberate is the whole of this one, and each answer is decidable from the declaration alone.

A marker interface is a real pattern and is never reported. interface IAggregateRoot { } is how a codebase tags types for a generic constraint, for assembly scanning, or for a dispatcher — and an interface is the only correct shape for that, because it is the only one a type can adopt without changing what it inherits from. Every empty interface is out of scope, no further test.

A marker attribute is never reported either, and it does not need to be recognised as one: any declaration carrying an attribute list, or any declaration with a base list, is exempt — and every attribute type has at least one of the two. That also covers [JsonSerializable]-style declarations whose whole purpose is to be read by a generator, and [ApiController]-style types whose behaviour is entirely in a framework.

A base list is an exemption on its own. class StringList : List<string> { } names a closed generic, class SqlOrderRepository : RepositoryBase<Order> { } is a leaf of a closed hierarchy, and class TimeoutFailure : Failure { } is a case in a sealed-hierarchy discriminated union — three shapes where the declaration carries all its meaning in the base list and the empty body is correct. ⚠ This also puts an empty exception type, which the proposal wanted reported, out of scope. class NotFoundException : Exception { } is a real complaint — the type cannot carry a message — but it is CA1032's complaint, it is stated better there, and separating "an exception with no constructors" from "a leaf of a closed hierarchy" needs semantics this rule does not have.

`partial` is never reported. The other part may be in another file, or may not exist yet because a generator writes it. This single exemption is what keeps the rule out of every source-generated codebase.

A generic empty type is never reported. class Metres { } used as Quantity<Metres> is a phantom type, and class Marker<T> { } is the generic version of one; a type parameter is a strong signal that the type exists to be named rather than instantiated.

A bodyless `record Foo;` is never reported. The semicolon form exists precisely to declare a complete type with nothing in it — a unit or a message in a message-based codebase — so writing one is a statement rather than an omission. record Foo { }, with braces around nothing, is reported.

⚠ The shape that remains genuinely ambiguous is the non-generic phantom type: sealed class Metres { } with no base and no attribute, used only as a type argument. It is reported, and it is a false positive. Deciding otherwise would need to know every use of the type, which is a whole-compilation question and this rule is syntactic by design. Suppress it or baseline it; the rule ships at suggestion for this reason.

⚠ No fix. Deleting a type is not a mechanical edit — something may name it, including code the compilation cannot see, such as reflection, a DI registration by name, or a serialised payload. Filling it in is not mechanical either. The finding says look at this; it does not say what to do.
